speechtext: The House resumed from Tuesday, September 13, consideration of Bill C-110, to amend the Export Development Act, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Hon. Members will remember that Motion No. 2 and Motion No. 4 were ruled out of order last Tuesday. The House will now proceed to Motion No. 3 and Motion No. 5 which are grouped for debate but will be voted on separately.
[DOT]	(mo)

Motion No. 3.
That Bill C-l 10, an Act to amend the Export Development Act, be amended in Clause 5 by striking out lines 23 to 26 at page 3 and substituting the following therefor:
"11.(1) The authorized capital of the Corporation is one billion one hundred dollars divided into ten million and one shares with a par value of one hundred dollars each."
Motion No. 5.
That Bill C-l 10, an Act to amend the Export Development Act, be amended in Clause 7 by striking out lines 39 to 41 at page 3 and lines I and 2 at page 4 and substituting the following therefor:
"14. The aggregate amount of borrowings of the Corporation pursuant to sections 12 and 13 shall not exceed the amount equal to ten times the aggregate of the paid in capital and earned surplus in the accounts of the Corporation."
He said: The effect of the amendments before us today, Mr. Speaker, is to control the borrowing authority of this corporation. The House will recall that when we considered this Bill on Tuesday last, we dealt with the question of whether the corporation should be controlled by independent, private enterprise people on its board of directors. That, apparently, was not the real wish of the Government.
Now we have a worse situation the question of control over the corporation. In the Export Development Bill there is a provision that the corporation have an authorized capital of $1 billion. Then Clause 11 of the Bill provides that the corporation can borrow ten times its authorized capital, so at the
present time the corporation could borrow on its own account, without ever coming to Parliament, an amount of $10 billion. It does not matter how much money is subscribed to the corporation by the Government; the essence of the problem is that if the Government gives the corporation the authority to have authorized capitalization, from then on the borrowing of the corporation is not tied to the money in its bank account. It is not tied to the capital and surplus actually paid into the corporation but is tied only to its authorized capital. That is the most ridiculous situation one could ever imagine, Mr. Speaker. The reason for the amendment is to ensure that under no circumstances are we going to allow borrowing against just authorized capital. What we must insist upon, if we are going to have any sense of direction in this corporation at all, is borrowing against subscribed capital or earned surplus.
The borrowing or leverage arrangements of trust companies, banks and the like are tied to the subscribed capital and surplus. For example, we will allow a trust company to borrow 20 times against its paid-in capital and surplus but we will not allow a trust company to borrow against its authorized capital. The point is that you can incorporate a company for $1 million but you do not have to put the total, incorporated, authorized amount into the company till. When I began practising law these used to be called $3 companies; now they should be called $1 companies-you just put in enough to buy one share.
Essentially the Bill provides that you can borrow not ten times what you have in the company but ten times what the authority of the company is, no matter whether any money is paid into the treasury or any shares are subscribed. The only way that the House of Commons can responsibly control the borrowing activities of the Export Development Corporation is to control its authorized capital.
The House will recall that the Chair ruled Motion No. 4 out of order. I want to say to the Chair that I agree that the motion should have been ruled out of order. It was placed on the Order Paper only to point out to people reading it and understanding the Bill that what we really want is some sort of control over the borrowing of this corporation. The way to have that control is by the percentage of leverage against the paid-in capital and earned surplus of the corporation. We would be satisfied with ten times paid-in capital and earned surplus.
However, the Government does not want any controls on this corporation. The Government wants to be able to borrow without ever coming to Parliament for approval. The Government wants to be able to borrow against authorized capital

September 15, 1983
Export Development Act
and to give itself $10 billion additional borrowing authority, to borrow against the credit of the people of Canada, the taxpayers of Canada. This Government says: "Just increase the capitalization of the Export Development Corporation by increasing the authorized capital from $1 billion to $2 billion, and we get $10 billion more borrowing authority". Without ever coming to Parliament again, without this House ever having an aye, yea or nay as to how the Government borrows money, it receives the right to borrow $10 billion. That, Sir, is totally unacceptable.
We were elected to this place to control the borrowings, the taxing, the public purse, yet this Government in this legislation wants to take away that control and give it to a board of directors, largely civil servants, to do what it damned well feels like. That is unacceptable. No Member of Parliament can accept this provision in this Bill. The only way the amendment could be put is to alter the demand of the Government, and we have altered that demand. We have said: "Whereas you have $1 billion of authorized capital, pass this amendment and we will give you $1 billion plus $100, and that will control your borrowing. That will keep you in line, and that will show some discipline". This cannot continue. Parliament must have control over the money borrowed on the credit of Canada, and unless Parliament has that control, what is the point of Parliament?
The Minister may say: "Well, Parliament has control. If Parliament votes this $2 billion authorization, then Parliament in effect is authorizing $20 billion of borrowing authority in total, and, therefore, Parliament has the right to vote on $20 billion of borrowing authority". That is what we are asked to vote on. The trouble is that that borrowing authority goes on forever until it is used up and never again, until the corporation has borrowed its $20 billion, will we ever see any report or have any right to control the activities of this corporation.
This corporation has a tremendous lobby going for it. We all want to make sure that Canada exports goods, capital goods, because the export of goods means jobs. Heaven knows, Canadians are looking for places to work, worth-while work, good work, and exports of goods mean jobs for Canadians. But what jobs are created for Canadians if the resources of Canada are squandered and wasted? While we might be able to finance at low rates goods for export to other countries, it is we Canadians who must use our work and effort to pay for those subsidized rates.
Somewhere along the line there has to be a balance and there is no evidence presented in any of the committee reports to indicate how competent the directors of this corporation have been in financing and building up Canada's trade. Indeed, not long ago we had nearly 6 per cent of world trade; we are now approaching 3 per cent.
The Government says this money is needed to finance the export of capital goods. Sir, this corporation lent money to 62 companies in Canada last year to finance sales of trade goods overseas. Half the money went to two companies. In its
analysis of where we should be going, the Economic Council of Canada made some serious criticisms of this corporation and how it operates. Professor Andre Raynauld, who was head of the Economic Council of Canada at one point, has said that this corporation is out of control. What we have to do, Sir, is put some parliamentary control back in place. We cannot go on any longer allowing a board of directors to borrow almost any amount against authorized capital without any control by Parliament.

Mr. Speaker, I rise with some enthusiasm to support this motion before the House. I believe what we are talking about here is absolutely critical to the future of Canada's export trade and whether or not we are going to become active players on the world trading stage.
1 must say that past performance of the EDC does not encourage one to be enthusiastic about the future role of Canada in the international marketplace. As my friend has pointed out, the funds from the EDC which were to assist Canadian firms to enter the international marketplace have not been handed out in a fair and equitable fashion. In other words, when 50 per cent of all the funds go to two large Canadian companies, and we all know of dozens and dozens of Canadian firms who would enjoy getting involved in the export marketplace and are unable to access those funds, I say that the EDC is not fulfilling the mandate originally given to it to encourage Canadian firms to operate in the international marketplace.
I like this particular motion, Mr. Speaker, because it brings some accountability to this Crown corporation. I believe it is crucial that the EDC become more active because I can recall a number of contracts where the Canadian firm has been the lowest bidder and these contracts could have provided hundreds and hundreds of jobs to certain parts of Canada; yet we lost those contracts because of the financing arrangements other bidders were able to produce that were better than what Canada could produce through the EDC.
1 believe the EDC must appear before the appropriate committee of Parliament on a regular basis to explain its behaviour during these critical times. It has now lost any real sense of what is required of it. It has become very much unaccountable for its deeds. I believe the time has come when Members of Parliament must not only request but indeed demand more accountability from Crown corporations and Government departments per se. The reason I say that is that all of us have numerous examples where Government departments and bureaucrats have really lost sight of what their role is.
I want to use a typical but specific example in this context. The middle of July, 1983 saw a major washout of the Trans-Canada Highway in the Rogers Pass area of British Columbia. That is to be expected in the mountain passes of Canada, in that very rugged part of our country, but because of a closure which lasted for many days, businesses that depend upon the movement of travellers through this country for only a few weeks of the year saw that livelihood fall away around them as
September 15, 1983

travellers going east and west simply stopped for too many days.
There were accusations hurled about at the time that the officials in Parks Canada did not have an action plan to put into place to create a bridge which would stop this closure. The co-operation between provincial and federal authorities could have been considerably better. As a result, so many people in tourist and hospitality businesses as well as related small businesses providing the necessary infrastructure, the restaurants, the laundries, the entertainment facilities and so on, lost that crucial piece of business during that important season, at this critical time in Canada's economic history, so that today there is evidence of number of bankruptcies that would not normally have occurred.
Of more importance is the fact that this situation need not have occurred had officials representing Parks Canada acted more appropriately and with more haste with regard to the concerns of those surrounding businesses, and if the people that they employ had kept these concerns more in the forefront of their decision-making.
1 raise this matter because I raised it with the Minister responsible. Of course, there was no response; he just simply ignored this Member of Parliament from western Canada who is speaking out on behalf of hundreds of businesses that have been devastated in that particular area of the country.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I regret the necessity of interrupting the Hon. Member. The point he is making is interesting, but perhaps he could indicate to the Chair in what way it is related to the two motions now before the House.

You bet, Mr. Speaker, 1 certainly will do just that. What we are discussing in this particular motion concerns bringing some accountability to Canada's Crown corporations.
1 say that because, unquestionably, a situation has developed in our country that has resulted in Government per se being too far removed from the real world. Here we are asking to control the borrowing authority. We are simply asking, as Members of Parliament concerned about export trade, about the Export Development Corporation, that if that corporation, in the best interests of Canadians, wishes to have more funds at its disposal to assist Canadian firms and workers, that it come to Parliament and make its case. That is all we are asking, that this Crown corporation, which is critical to Canada's future, come to Canada's Parliament and make a case for more funds. If it made the case, its request would be granted.
Over the years we have seen the Export Development Corporation of Canada becoming rather arrogant. We have seen this corporation losing sight of its real mandate. When one hears that in the last year the Export Development Corporation assisted only some 60 firms in this country, then 1 believe that in terms of Canada playing its role on the overseas economic stage, one realizes that we have missed that opportunity. If there is one thing that we must do in this country, it is
Export Development Act
to bolster up that Crown corporation, to give it support as a Parliament.
When I hear the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Lumley) telling me that we will open our floodgates and encourage more relationships between Canada and the U.S. in the field of foreign trade, I begin to worry. To add even more foreign trade to what is already going to the United States is essentially putting more of our eggs in that single basket. It is in Canada's interest to open up overseas markets in Europe, Southeast Asia and the Middle East and not necessarily to increase trade with the United States.
Another point which I believe needs to be made while talking about the Export Development Corporation is that if freer trade with the United States is opened up, there will be a migration of American branch plants out of this country. In other words, rather than create more jobs and more opportunities in this country, we will see a net job loss in Canada as a result of liberalizing trade with the United States. Many American subsidiaries are operating in Canada now simply to get around our existing tariff walls and the like. We will see at net loss of jobs perhaps at a level that would astound most Canadians.
In closing, I suggest that there is no shortage of examples of the necessity of Government departments-Crown corporations more specifically-becoming more accountable to the people of Canada through Canada's Parliament. This motion simply asks for more accountability. I do not believe there are many Members of the House of Commons who do not feel that so many of our Crown corporations are out of control and not necessarily acting in the best interests of Canadians and Canadian workers. There is very little difference between the Crown corporation and the corporation next door. Surely if we are going to have Crown corporations there must be more reason for their existence than simply creating a corporation to compete with fellow corporations in both the national and international marketplace. Therefore, I support this motion which is before the House today because it attempts to bring more accountability to Canada's Crown corporations.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. Before I recognize the next speaker, the Chair feels that this is a good time at the resumption of our session to remind Hon. Members that they should not cross the floor between the Member speaking and the Chair. I assume this is meant as a courtesy to the Member who is speaking so that he can command the undivided attention of the Chair.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak on Motion No. 3. Having spent the morning reading "The Rocky Road to the 1990s", I suggest that the Government is putting the cart before the horse. It is asking Parliament to increase its borrowings by approximately 2.5 times before it sets forth an economic policy which indicates what we will be trading. Our objection through Motion No. 3 is that the Government is asking for too much on a carte blanche basis.

September 15, 1983
Export Development Act
The Government is trying to use its letters of comfort which it has used in the past when going ahead to issue funds out of the treasury without ever coming to this Parliament. This is the same procedure.
The Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) has simply requested that, instead of proceeding with $2 billion paid-in capital, to go to $1 billion and $100. The reason for this is that Crown corporations presently have adequate funds for all potential trades. We are simply requesting, as we have on a number of Bills, that appropriations come before the House of Commons. This is too global in approach; we want more specific terms of reference. We want to know what the Government has done with what we have allowed it to spend before it proceeds to spend on a carte blanche basis money of which we are not aware and which even the Auditor General has difficulty finding. I do not refer to the Export Development Corporation in this regard.
Before continuing 1 would like to commend the Export Development Corporation. 1 recently had a case in my riding where a small company was having difficulty arranging financing. If the bank took on the finance it came out of the owner's credit loan from that bank. A senior vice-president of the Export Development Corporation stepped in at my request and has resolved the problem to his satisfaction. I appreciate that type of co-operation extended by Government departments to the Opposition.
Furthermore, I believe this is an area where the Export Development Corporation can be of great benefit to this country. While there is little likelihood of large corporations being developed, there is greater potential for the development of smaller corporations. Due to today's global trading, a small corporation can exist only when a large portion of its output goes to international trade. The problem does not lie so much with the Government but with many people in the country who are not aware of what is available to assist them in merchandising their products.
I would also point out that many small organizations have difficulty arranging loans because they do not have the lobby groups representing them or large corporate sectors acting on their behalf. Therefore they must be assisted through the Department of DRIE, formerly Industry, Trade and Commerce.
With respect to Motion No. 3, I believe the Government is going too far when asking for this much of an increase at this time. We are losing track of what $1 billion is. A billion dollars is $1,000 million. This increase which permits the Government to go $10,000 million into debt is a tremendous amount of money for the House to give carte blanche. The entire Bill permits the Government to borrow up to $60 billion. That is approximately one-third of our total national debt according to the latest figures. 1 believe that rapidly increasing these amounts for the benefit of one sector will leave nothing for other sectors.
These increases should be made on an annual or semi-annual basis. Perhaps we could discuss it in a limited debate, so that if there is a reasonable amount being requested and we
understand its purpose and what the corporation will do, it could be acceptable. However, we object to increases in 2.5 multiples in order to assist the Minister so that he will not have to return to the House.
He did make a point to me which 1 can acknowledge. He said: "When you are in Government you will not have to come in front of the House". He is a Member who realizes that they are in their dying days of Government and that this will be of benefit to Canadians through a great Party, the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada.
Let me talk about Motion No. 5 for a moment. This method is logical, reasonable and used in every financial institution in Canada. They not only take their paid-in capital; it is based on paid-in capital together with earned surplus. This gives them an even broader base on which to borrow funds. It goes beyond $20 billion if we allow this provision, which we are not going to. It gives EDC the right to borrow ten times $1 billion plus ten times the earned surplus.
I have to speak in favour of the Hon. Member's motion. It is economically sound. 1 believe the Auditor General would approve of this approach. 1 believe all of Canada will approve of this approach. 1 know the Provinces feel we have gone too far. Let us take a look at this particular allegation. Have the Provinces been brought into the discussion? My Province accounts for approximately 50 per cent of the funds required by EDC. Has Ontario been brought in? Has the matter been discussed with the Deputy Minister or the Minister of Industry and Trade for the Province of Ontario? 1 am sure this Province would agree that this is asking too much at one time.
We have to stop running and start walking. We have to start analysing. We have to start looking at where we have been. What has got us into this mess today? The paper to which I have referred this morning "The Rocky Road to the 1990s" written by the Minister of State for Economic Development (Mr. Johnston), has brought it all out. He said that FIRA has been a stumbling block. He said the National Energy Program has been a stumbling block. He enumerates all the things this Government has done in the last 15 years which have caused this severe recession and severe unemployment.
The Government is putting the cart before the horse. The Government must present to this Parliament an economic policy that will broaden international trade. The Government must show this Parliament how it will create jobs. The Government has not yet done anything despite its statements and suggestions from the opposition.
We must defeat this Bill because of this section. The Minister should be reasonable. He should reduce the amount requested and ask for a reasonable amount, the amount required at this time. When he requires more, he should come back to this House of Commons and make his request.

Mr. Speaker, 1 would say that the Bill before the House today suffers from a
September 15, 1983

disease that has become part and parcel of the philosophy of this administration, namely, inflation.

This is not a new Bill. When this Bill was drafted Cabinet approved the proposals with regard to changes to the Export Development Act. Inflation was rushing along rampant at a rate between 10 per cent and 12 per cent per annum. If that had continued then, of course, in five or eight years it blows totals all out of proportion.
That is why we have this proposal for $2 billion in authorized capital. There is no need for that. Who is going to take up that capitalization? Will it be farmed out to CDIC as well for operation? I am sorry 1 do not have last year's annual statement here to see if there is an accumulated surplus, but we should see the leverage that is available to the EDC for its borrowings. My colleagues the Hon. Members from Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) and Ontario (Mr. Fennell) have said that if these proposals ultimately go through it is conceivable that the Export Development Agency could borrow up to $60 billion or even, if you want to cut it back, $50 billion. If you have one corporation able to do that, there goes parliamentary control immediately. There is no control whatsoever.
What about considering the annual report? That is hindsight on operations two years ago. There is a psychosis in the bureaucracy of this Government that it should not be accountable to Parliament. This administration supinely follows that dictum. Parliament represents the people of Canada and has the ultimate authority. The way legislation has been brought forward, and this particular piece of legislation is a case in point, it removes from Parliament one more area of control. The general taxpayers of the country are not aware of that. Polls say that Parliament, to them, is of no great concern. First, most people do not understand Parliament. Second, as long as nobody has a Bunsen burner, or to put it another way, to put an old matchstick on their soul, they are not concerned. Nobody is borrowing their particular odds. But on the whole, when people ask about the expenditures and the demands of Government upon the average taxpayer, is it realized that almost 50 cents out of every dollar earned in Canada goes to Government at some level?
The recipients of Government largesse are not the ones who will complain. But the ones who are producing, the salaried people, the hourly-rated people-I do not care where they are-are being squeezed and squeezed beyond all reason. This Bill is part of that philosophy. It is Government, big Government. EDA is just part of the apparatus; it is just one of the Crown corporations.
We can go through the list of Crown corporations. There is no control. They do not want control. They are bureaucrats of the Government's own making and they tell Government what should be done and the public be damned. I have a classic example. I know a number of officials in this corporation, many of them very able men. I am not being patronizing when I say that. However, the corporation does not require this authorization. It does not require this power. It should come to Parliament and explain the situation if it needs more author-
Export Development Act
ity. With this Bill, the corporation will not have to come back to Parliament for authorization or accountability until the year 2050, if ever.
This is one of the most glaring and outrageous examples of bureaucratic gall. My colleague's amendment states $100 more, one more share. This is a procedural tactic so that we can debate this section. I attended the committee hearings but I have not yet seen the case made for an increase in capital. Right now there is unissued capital. There is authority in subsequent clauses to borrow. In his other amendments, my colleague has given a balance. He states ten times leverage, which is what was asked, but we have added surplus to the outstanding capital which is not included in the government's proposal.
I implore Hon. Members, if there is any time when we can be serious and come back down to earth, it is to accept my colleague's amendment. The Government's proposals with regard to the share structure and the potential volume of borrowings by the EDC are just not acceptable. They are ludicrous.

Mr. Speaker, I rise with some concern regarding what is being asked by the Government as far as the Export Development Corporation is concerned. The Hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) made an excellent argument regarding our concern about what is being asked for in this Bill.
The Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) has put forward very reasoned and reasonable amendments. According to the 1982 annual report, the corporation has substantial retained earnings. In 1982 it accounted for $186.1 million of shareholders' equity, which I presume can be re-borrowed. The Government of Canada increased its budget for share capital during that year by $115 million, bringing the total to $465 million. During that year, EDC borrowed $787 million through a mix of public issues and private placements in the international marketplace.
Given its present authority, it does not need anywhere near the amount being asked for in this Bill. It is as if the Minister is saying to Members of Parliament: "Gee, we don't want to bother you too much, you are too busy; as a result, we will ask for sufficient capital for years and years into the future".
Having been a Member of Parliament for a number of years, I would like to be bothered more. Members have lost control over Crown corporations which have been created in abundance in the last number of years and, as mentioned by my colleague, we have lost control over the public purse.
The deficit is incomprehensible, not only to those in my constituency but I am sure to constituents all across the country. We are getting into the $30 billion range. Last year it was over $20 billion. In his budget the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) said in a very optimistic fashion that if this Government is allowed to continue, it will be over $20 billion for the next five years.

September 15, 1983
Export Development Act
Why should we be concerned when in this Bill the Government is just asking for authority to increase the authorized capital of the corporation from $1 billion to $2 billion? It is because when we look deeper we find there is the opportunity to borrow ten times that authorized capital. In effect, we are adding $10 billion to the borrowing authority of this corporation, something that it has shown it does not require.
It would be nice if the officials of the corporation could come before Parliament when the estimates are being considered. They could tell us whether the authority is inadequate. If that was the case, it would mean that exports from this country were moving at a very rapid rate and that businesses, large and small, require that kind of financing being made available to this corporation in order to get into world markets.
We all recognize that world trade is very difficult, particularly in a recession. Many countries have a high rate of advanced manufacturing capabilities. They compete with us in the world markets. Many of those countries have substantially more amounts of capital available than we do and can move into those markets. Therefore, we require a very efficient and capable corporation to assist businesses in this country to move up into those markets.
The value of EDC is not being questioned. What is being questioned is the authority of Parliament to have that corporation come before us and give us the reasons why we ought to move more of the taxpayers' money into that account. That is what is being questioned.
When we look at the statistics for world trade, it is depressing to note that we are not advancing our percentage of world trade as we should be. We are falling behind our traditional proportion, dropping from 6 per cent to 3 per cent. This is very noticeable in the agricultural sector. We used to have a large share of the world market, well over 25 per cent of the world grain market in exports. That has dropped substantially and is now well under 20 per cent. At the same time the Americans, one of our chief competitors, have increased their share of world trade from something in the neighbourhood of 25 per cent to well over 50 per cent. That has been accomplished by very hard-nosed selling, bargaining and the use of export credit.
We in the agricultural sector have pleaded with the Export Development Corporation to assist us in that area, but very little assistance has been forthcoming. If you look at the record for last year, only 62 companies were assisted, with most of the money going to the manufacturing sector. What, then, do we have? We have now created another Crown corporation to deal with agriculture, Canagrex. Looking at the statement of this corporation, one finds that it had 613 employees to contract 62 loans last year. There were one and a half employees for each insurance account. It seems to me, looking at those statistics, that there would be sufficient employees to allow for expansion and that we would not need another corporation with another $12 billion worth of capital from Government assigned to it to create another group of employees to do exactly what this corporation should be doing.
That is why the amendment that is before us is so important. It is important so that we as Members of Parliament, the stewards of the taxpayers' money, can ask in-depth questions dealing with how these corporations are operating, why they require the staff levels they do have and why this corporation requires offices in five cities across the country to do so little business-although the value of the business it does do is great; and why, with all that capital, they showed only about $1 million profit last year.
Perhaps the answer to some of these questions can be found in the way those corporations operate. The requirement for efficiency in a Crown corporation does not seem to be as great as the requirement for efficiency in the private sector. That is why the amendment that was lost on Tuesday was so important. It proposed having the private sector more involved in the operation of this corporation because the private sector has learned how to be lean and efficient and to operate in a proper business manner.
We are saying that this corporation should be the vehicle to assist us in international trade. We would like to see the private sector more involved. We believe that this corporation ought to come to Parliament once in a while when it is asking for refuelling in order that we can decide whether it needs its oil changed or whether we should just tune it up a little bit.
Mr. Speaker, what we are dealing with and what we are not dealing with needs to be established lest there be any misunderstanding.
That is a good idea.
Obviously, what we are not dealing with is the question of whether or not export is of value.
It is.

What is not at issue is that particular question.
You will note, Mr. Speaker, that over the weekend the members of this caucus met at Mont Ste-Marie. The members of the NDP caucus, of course, met at Mount St. Helen's and they are now continuing to blow their top.
What is at issue is the question of accountability and the question of control. Essentially, that is all that is at issue. That issue is of such magnitude that it raises the hackles of the Auditor General of Canada to the point where three Auditor Generals have worked on the theory that the Government has lost or is near losing control of the public purse.
Control of the public purse is the reason for Parliament's existence. That reason dates back to the time of King Charles and the debates that then took place and the referendums thereafter dealing with who would have control of the purse of Parliament. The question of parliamentary control and where this fundamental power exists is central to the whole issue. If power is to reside in the people of a democracy, then they must exercise their power through their representatives in Parliament. If any sum of money, Mr. Speaker, irrespective of its
September 15, 1983

size, is out of the public eye and out of the control of the people's representatives, then democracy has been diminished and Parliament has been thwarted.
According to Auditor General Kenneth Dye, what exists today is a situation in which the massive growth of corporations owned by the federal Government has created a $34 billion layer of Government that is largely hidden from public view and not properly accountable to Parliament. In the particular amendment before the House of Commons today, we are essentially attempting to make it impossible for one more Crown corporation to borrow without telling the people of Canada why it needs some $10 billion.
The other issue that must be stressed is that need has not been established. The amount of borrowing power that is available today to the Export Development Corporation has not been utilized to its fullest extent. It does not spend the amount it asks for, yet if the amendment is not accepted, we are allowing it to borrow twice as much. Surely no corporation should be given a blank cheque for borrowing to the maximum of $10 billion unless it comes to the people's representatives to demonstrate need. If need cannot be demonstrated, blank cheques up to $10 billion should not be granted.
One of the great difficulties that we face in a democracy today is that people have become insulated and shockproofed through ignorance of what numbers actually mean. Numeral names without relationships remain mere names. What is a billion? What is a trillion?
The very first experience I had as a Member of Parliament in 1974 in a House of Commons committee was when I was on the energy committee and Dome Petroleum were arguing that they could not advance certain projects on the northern Arctic coast because there was not a large enough volume of gas present. At that time I asked what the known reserves were. The witness said that it was 16 trillion cubic feet. 1 asked him how large reserves had to be before he could develop them, and he said 20 trillion cubic feet. Using simple mathematics, 16 from 20 means that he was only four short. The fundamental question was, what is a trillion?
We ask that question today. Pieces of paper are covered with notations showing how many billions of dollars we are in debt, and the public is insulated. It really does not matter to the average Canadian whether we are $34 billion, $10 billion or $134 billion in debt because the numbers are meaningless.
A million dollars in $1 bills laid end to end will go from where you are, Mr. Speaker, to a community 80 miles away. A billion dollars in $1 bills laid end to end will go from Vancouver to Halifax and back two and a half times. We are allowing the Export Development Corporation to ask for ten times that amount without once demonstrating need.
Surely if Parliament is to discharge its responsibility to the people, then control must be exercised. As reported in an article in The Globe and Mail:
Mr. Dye said that, this year, he had been able to get all of the information he required for his audit but that some of it was obtained only with great difficulty. Information on the purchase of Petrofina by Petro-Canada was not easily
Export Development Act
obtained for his audit of the Energy Department or on GN Marine for his audit of Transport Canada, he said.
As another Member mentioned earlier, when it comes to Crown corporations there is a feeling that it is the money of the Canadian, people that is involved. In more than one audit of the Government of Canada, the Auditor General has said that he has great difficulty finding out the spending of various departments and that extends through Crown corporations. Surely it is the obligation of Parliament, the principal court of the land, to make sure that there is a visible accounting of the people's money. The Auditor General should not have a difficult time but, rather, should have an easy time identifying the need and ensuring that there is control and accountability.
The report in The Globe and Mail of Wednesday, December 8, 1982 went on to say:
Even when Parliamentary safeguards are in place. Crown corporations do not always follow them, the report said. In 1981, for instance. Air Canada was required to tell the federal Treasury Board, which watches over public spending, of any plans to make a major investment.
On Sept. 4. Air Canada spent $4.5 million to buy into another aviation company. It notified the Treasury Board, the report said, on Sept. 3.
According to the rules, the relevant department must be informed in advance, yet $4.5 million was spent in one day, less than 24 hours' notice having been given.
With assets of approximately $67 billion, liabilities of over $57 billion, annual expenses of over $30 billion and with more employees than Government departments, the Auditor General came to the conclusion that Crown corporations require an improved framework to make them accountable to Parliament and to the Government.
What my colleague is asking is that a measure of the accountability requested by the Auditor General be required. Whether the average Canadian understands what a billion dollars is or not, he knows that the country is spending foolishly and beyond its capacity. That accountability must be provided, and to that end I submit that the amendment should be passed.
I see that you are making some gesture toward me, Mr. Speaker. Are you telling me that my time is nigh? That is too bad, because I have only dealt with the first few dollars and we have a billion or ten to go.

Mr. Speaker, the authorized capital of the Export Development Corporation will increase from $1 billion to $2 billion as stated in Bill C-110. The ceiling for loans and insurance written under the authority of the EDC, the corporate account, will rise to $20 billion from $10 billion.
Whenever the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) concurs in a recommendation from the board, the Government can contribute capital to the corporation. There is no parliamentary control on contributions; the Government just puts up the money. The Minister of Finance has the absolute right to subscribe to the capital of the Export Development Corporation. The Government can make loan advances that are

September 15, 1983
Export Development Act
deemed not to be of a commercial or proper risk by the board of directors. The Government will, if these amendments are passed the way they are, be entitled to up to $10 billion for unacceptable loans. This kind of accountability cannot be allowed to continue. Parliament and Parliament alone should have control of the public purse.
Crown corporations are not well received by the Canadian public. Lack of praise is not unfounded. Prime examples are Canadair and de Havilland. Canadians associate Crown corporations with the glaring problem of accountability to Parliament for expenditures, which, of course, are funded by taxpayers' dollars.
An extensive study done by the Economic Council of Canada strongly criticized the corporations. Many improvements need to be made. The Export Development Corporation must be made accountable for its actions, funds and liabilities. When the Government wants to put capital in the corporation the Government should produce a new estimate and money vote allowing it to purchase shares in the corporation. At the present time, capital is injected into the corporation by the Minister of Finance approving a request from the board of directors, without a parliamentary aye, yes or no.
The provision in the existing Act allowing for a special fund where the Government can take up loans and advances that do not meet EDC specifications should either be abolished or, in the alternative, no Governor in Council advance should be made without the approval of Parliament. The amendments increasing the fund available for Governor in Council advances to $10 billion should be eliminated. The present provisions of the Act allow for $2.5 billion of Governor in Council advances of which roughly $700 million of the authority is used.
At the present time EDC has borrowing authority of $10 billion. As of December 31, 1982 it had used only approximately $4.5 billion of its authority.
Mr. Speaker, the Government should support Motions Nos. 3 and 5 as tabled by the Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) so that there will be proper accountability in this Crown corporation.

Mr. Speaker, it is incomprehensible that a so-called responsible Government should present legislation such as this to Parliament. I well remember when I first came to the House of Commons that the ceiling on the UIC fund was $800 million. We encouraged the Government of the day to put a ceiling on the fund so that there would be some form of accountability to Parliament but it did not see fit to do so. As a result, after 11 years the UIC fund now spends $12 billion. That is why it is so important that somehow or other we hold the Government accountable for a Crown corporation. This is of fundamental importance to our democratic way of life. If we do not accomplish that, then the whole parliamentary system will break down. Economic freedom will be lost if corporations like this are not held accountable for their actions. It is this sort of thing that makes Canadians very apprehensive.
Years ago Canadians never asked: "What are we going to do about our national debt or about our Crown corporations?" Today, however, they find that governments are allowing the situation to develop where Crown corporations can borrow money in the markets of the world, perhaps at a favourable rate, and they use that money in a way that the Canadian people object to.
Perhaps the best example I can give is that last summer the Export Development Corporation was borrowing money at 9.875 per cent. At the present time the proposed requirements of the Farm Credit Corporation have been cut back by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde). He did this unilaterally. Legislation was passed in this House in the spring which would allow the Farm Credit Corporation to borrow up to $600 million on the money markets of the world. However, the Minister of Finance cut back that amount to $250 million. If ever there was a time in Canadian history in which the farmers require money, it is now; yet there has been a cutback by the Minister of Finance. Here we have the Government allowing a Crown corporation to enter into, shall we say, dubious loans without the scrutiny of Parliament. This is what this exercise is all about. We have to be able to hold the Government responsible, and the only way in which the Canadian taxpayer or the Canadian citizen can hold the Government at bay on any of these issues is through the Parliament of Canada.
Through this legislation which is being proposed we are losing that control. We do have a medium of control if this amendment presented by my hon. colleague is accepted and it is important that Parliament has that control. I am not speaking just as a member of the opposition; I am speaking as a member of a political party which feels it is a government in waiting and that within several months, possibly, it will be taking power. We anticipate that we can live within those restraints, and in bringing in that kind of legislation we are going to give confidence to the Canadian taxpayer, confidence in the system which is not there at the present time.
Yesterday, an individual from the farm survival group who is living in Ontario told me he had lost faith in Canada, in the parliamentary system and in politicians. The only way, Mr. Speaker, that we are going to re-establish that faith in the minds of the Canadian electorate is to bring in responsible legislation so that Canadians know that what is being done is done for their benefit. We are not talking about exporting. The importance to Canada of exporting has been emphasized time and time again, Mr. Speaker. However, we must have a degree of fairness in these deals. We have the right to know what has been happening. We have to know what actually is taking place. We have to know that the Export Development Corporation is going to be held responsible.
There is a human characteristic which possibly is evident in all of us, whether we be Parliamentarians or otherwise; we all like to build empires. I have a feeling that within the Export Development Corporation there is a great deal of empire building taking place. Why would one need 613 employees to
September 1 5, 1983

deal with approximately 62 applications last year? That is ten individuals for one application all year. Does this really make sense to you, Mr. Speaker? It certainly does not to me. There were applications for 900 insurance policies last year. That is one and one half insurance policies for each individual all year. This is not just for the current period of time spent working on them, but this is for all year. I believe, Mr. Speaker, we should be able to see just exactly what is happening there. If ever we are going to have a frugal government, if ever we are going to have a frugal operation within our way of life, then we have to be able to hold these Crown corporations accountable to the Canadian people. Otherwise, we find the system is taking too much out of the public purse and there is not enough left for private business and the people in private enterprise.
I mentioned earlier that the Export Development Corporation was able to borrow money last summer for 9.875 per cent.
I would like to know how it was done. I commend them for it. But why today, if the Export Development Corporation can borrow money at that percentage rate, has the interest rate for the Farm Credit Corporation gone up to 13.5 per cent? I feel that in a great many cases our own private businesses and our own Canadian people are suffering as a consequence of what the Crown corporation is doing.
We have to recognize that the Government in its wisdom can enter into agreements which the Export Development Corporation cannot do, and the best example 1 can give is the $295 million which was really loaned to New York City by the Crown corporation. It was not enough; it fell short of the Bombardier contract. The Government of Canada guaranteed another $627 million to finance LRC in the City of New York. If we can do that for the City of New York-this is all done at 9 per cent interest-why can we not do something like that for our own people in small business? Why can we not do it for the farmers? Why did this individual who was in my office yesterday have to pay 13.5 per cent for his financing while at the same time this situation is happening? These are things which I believe the Canadian people should have an opportunity to take a look at. We have to know exactly whether or not we are getting value for our money with the operation of EDC.
I see, Mr. Speaker, my time is up. I thank you for the opportunity to be able to present my case before you at this time.

Mr. Speaker, I have been listening to the debate today and I support the lack of necessity for increasing the capital of the Export Development Corporation to any great extent. The argument advanced by the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shus-wap (Mr. Riis) that the corporation should be more accountable to Parliament makes sense to me. I agree with the arguments advanced by several Hon. Members in my own party to the effect that one gets more efficiency in other ways than just simply by having a large board of directors and making available all this money.
When 1 spoke on one of the earlier motions I made the argument that the only real competition today between trading nations is in the field of the cost of capital or the lending rate.
Export Development Act
We have the ridiculous situation, when one is operating a government-run development corporation, of having that development corporation borrow from the treasury of Canada, which has to go into the markets of Canada and collect the money at 11 per cent and 12 per cent. Then in order to compete with the other trading nations of the world the corporation must provide concessional interest rates. It has to do this to stay in business.
I spoke the other day of the necessity of matching other countries on the interest rate, but going out in Canada in a way which will provide money at half the current interest rates. We have made clear here in the House over the last two or three years how it can be done, and which we made clear in the budget for 1980 can be done by enunciating the principle of the Small Business Development Bond. What I am going to do today is to refer to some practical experience which 1 have had and which deals with this very subject.
One of the great opportunities that exists for Canadians today is in the field of trade. We are good at it. For one reason or another very few nations of the world have any political hostility to us, and this gives us a great advantage. But more than that is required. Modern trade is a new subject for governments and for most of our businesses. We need an approach different from what we had in the past. For instance, the approach to a socialist nation is vastly different than that to a private enterprise nation. All our thinking here is to simply set up a development corporation that can only think of competing by lending money. I am saying there is a much cheaper and more effective way of achieving this goal.
Let me put on the record again what 1 think everyone in Canada knows who follows these matters, that our nation pioneered a new concept in 1960 by going out to a nation which had no money and saying: "Buy our products and we will give you three years to pay the money back; the interest rate will be the same as we have to pay in Canada".
But there was another ingredient of that policy which no one noticed. On behalf of the Canadian people and the then Canadian Government I gave my word to the Chinese Government that we in Canada would put all our efforts into helping the Chinese sell their goods around the world so they would have enough money to pay for our wheat. At first we dealt through correspondence and so on, but this was so slow that eventually I got an invitation to go there and talk to their minister directly about these techniques in 1964. I announced in the House, Mr. Speaker, that I was going at their invitation to discuss these matters. Out of these discussions came the idea that the best way to get around their difficulties was that there should be privately-run international trading companies set up in Canada and other countries which will come into China and find out what they could produce and go out and sell it for them. At the beginning there were just a few of those companies, mostly Japanese, but Canadian companies did get into it. I got the support of the banks to set up one here in Canada, but it was set up under such conditions that it was

September 15, 1983
Export Development Act
impossible to carry on. They simply wanted a "name" man at the head of these companies.
These are international trading companies, Mr. Speaker, and for efficiency they have to be very small, just a few people. Now, what big "name" man in Canada is going to come into a company which has to wait three or four years before they get any income? There is always a negative cash flow in the first three or four years of a private trading company. So eventually I set up a company based in the United States and we spent $400,000 running schools for Chinese technocrats and civil servants on how to utilize the products they wanted to buy. We spent time going all over the world trying to make arrangements to sell Chinese goods. The $400,000 was spent running the school in Peking for their technocrats and then they had the right to pick the product from which country they liked.
I do not have to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that when I started this business with China the total trade in and out was $400 million a year. Today it is $70 billion. This was done with almost no capital at all. I had estimated $1 million was required to carry us through but we did it for $400,000. 1 will not tell you what the income has been since, but the sales amount to billions of dollars every year and this company takes a very small fee which is very remunerative in the long run.
I give you this background because the idea is that it must be of mutual advantage to both sides. As a private company you can deal directly with that Government agency without thought of any political consequences either way. But if you have a Government agency dealing with it, you have to meet the political situation on both sides. What 1 am trying to get at here is that, sure, there are some political parts to play in this training operation, but that company succeeded way beyond my wildest expectations and did very well until Government began interfering. I do not want to tell you what the interference was, but it was as funny as Sam Hill.
If you are trying to develop trade in Canada, Mr. Speaker, use the technique of using your money in the development corporation to back up the fellows with ideas on how to do it. They will then bring more money back in than you can ever get trying to compete in this interest rate competition around the world.
As an example of what I want to suggest, you will find out very soon in international trade that if you follow the principle of mutual advantage and you are dealing with nations which have a long way to go on know-how, you have to spend a good deal of time and effort getting their know-how up to a level where they can make the right decision. You have to know a good deal about the needs of every nation. The needs of China, as an example, are well known. They are desperately short of fibre. Well, who can produce fibre? We can here in Canada. Brazil can. We can get it all over the world. The Chinese can produce it themselves. So any person dealing with a country like that which needs fibre has to think in terms of how their own people develop that fibre most efficiently and look for new markets. China still needs fibre in many forms and there is no one really making it in Canada. We have all this know-how in
fibre to go out and develop the capacity in that country and at the same time help meet their needs and their shortage of fibre right now. Increasingly western countries are going into China and doing this.
We have tremendous know-how in many fields. The greatest and most pressing need in China today is for water to drink and to wash themselves with in the cities. The water table below Peking has dropped six metres in the last 20 years. They are frightened. You do not go there with the idea of selling billions of dollars of some product; with one billion Chinese, one widget a piece makes a big deal. You go there with the idea of how you can help them make money. The way they can make money is by taking the tremendous know-how that Canada has and making sure that the amount of water they have can be used several times. Canada leads the world in its knowledge of recycling pure water. Take that knowledge, give them the ability to deliver a good standard of living and to go out and make money, and then just look at the opportunities for trade with all countries of the world, including Canada.
I want to conclude, Mr. Speaker, by saying that it is not the amount of money this corporation has; it is what this group of people do with it that counts. I am putting forward some practical advice in the hope that the Minister will make sure that his staff reads about this type of thing, and I will be glad to provide them with any details they want to know. If I cannot provide it, there are a thousand other guys who can.

Mr. Speaker, the discussion today is centring on amendments to the Export Development Act. This is not an attack on exports. No one questions the need to increase Canada's exports. Canada is capable of producing a great deal beyond its own needs. Canada thrives on exports. Canada must have exports. What we are discussing today is parliamentary responsibility, the responsibility of Parliament and Parliamentarians, over the expenditure of public funds. That is the discussion, despite the designation of the Bill.
My comments today are of a variety of sorts, but the first thing I would like to say relates to the form of the Bill as reprinted following the committee consideration. It is defective in a way which makes it rather complicated to deal with.
The original Bill, as brought forward at first reading on April 30, 1982 contained the text of the original Act face to face with the amendments thereto. I know that on page la of this Bill it states that the Bill as distributed in first reading form may be used for purposes of comparison. I would be happy to send the original text up to Your Honour so that you may see it, and I suggest that with all the automated equipment at our disposal, the amendments in the original text ought to be included in the Bill as amended, having gone through the committee. It is much simpler to have on the right-hand side of a bill the text of the section of the original Act that is being amended. Therefore, I think the procedure of not including the original text in the form as it comes from the
September 15, 1983

committee ought not to be continued. 1 think we should have that before us.
My second comment is as to language, unfortunately, dealing specifically with the amendment that we have before us. 1 am delighted to see that the proposed amendment as put forward by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), does not contain the bad English found in the original Act. The amendments that we have before us merely carry forward that bad English from the original text. Reading from the original text, referring to Clause 7, we find that Section 14 at present reads:
The aggregate amount of borrowings of the Coporation pursuant to sections 12 and 13 and outstanding shall not exceed an amount-
I am concerned about the words "and outstanding". I am sure that if Your Honour were to compare that with the French version, you would agree that the French text is comprehensible. It is understandable. The words "and oustanding" in English, because of their improper placing, make that particular Section idiotic. The French version is:

Le total non rembourse des emprunts de la Societe faits en application des articles 12 et 13-
That 1 can understand, but I certainly cannot make head or tail of this blunder in the English version.

The aggregate amount of borrowings of the Corporation pursuant to sections 12 and 13 and outstanding-
Why, in good sense, in ordinary Oxford English, does it not state, "the aggregate amount of outstanding borrowings"? It is as simple as that. That damned silly "and outstanding" is ridiculous. That was my second comment and I do hope that somewhere along the line the English version will conform more closely to the French text.
The Export Development Act was intended to create a corporation which would basically assist by insuring loans in order to enhance the opportunities of Canadians to export. It was an insurance scheme. I knew of its application while serving in Central America, where I had a fair amount of involvement with the Export Development Corporation in connection with a bid being made by what is now Northern Telecom to instal a microwave system of telecommunications from Panama right into Mexico. I will not mention the difficulties the company faced in dealing with the Export Development Corporation at that time concerning the underwriting of bids being put forward. That is a story in itself. However, at that particular time the Export Development Corporation was designed to insure against losses of loans made privately by the corporation. Advance of funds, that is loaning, was another matter. Now the Export Development Corporation has gone into the business of financing. Why, in the name of all decency and sensible business practice, is it not possible for a corporation that wants to export to go to the bank to borrow and then be allowed a tax concession for having taken that risk? That is the proper way to carry out business, not to run to the Government for another $1 billion
Export Development Act
at, as someone has said, 9,875 per cent when money elsewhere is at 11.75 per cent. We all remember what happened to Bombardier. It nearly lost the contract in New York because there was just a chance-and the anti-dumping tribunal of the United States, or whatever it is called, had to examine the matter very carefully-that Bombardier was gaining an advantage over an American corporation. It was the American corporation that raised the matter involving the installation of the system in New York. Bombardier could easily have gone to the private lending institutions in Canada, had its loan insured under the EDC and been able to write off its payments of interests, if you like, or make some sort of deal in the tax system. Bombardier could have stood up on its own feet and said: "We got that contract, we will fulfil it, and there is no danger whatsoever of anyone contesting it. The Canadian people, furthermore, are not financing it."
In Canada we must return to the situation where private corporations are proud to stand behind their product, to go out and sell it, to instal it and to have coverage of insurance for their loans at the bank and tax write-offs, if you like, for the interest that they may have to pay. Or some other formula; but I am not trying to rewrite the Tax Act. That is an approach which is completely forgotten in this particular Bill.
Another of our worries, returning to the matter of the responsibility of Parliament and Parliamentarians, concerns the expenditure of public funds. We have run into this matter all too often. It is time that we restored the responsibility of Parliament by putting a very firm cap on borrowings and a requirement that the Export Development Corporation return to Parliament from time to time in order to justify its expenditures. It should not become an autonomous creature in this country through Government action so that it can impose and load debts upon the next two, three or four generations, debts for which we ought to be ashamed.

Mr. Speaker, today we are discussing the amendment of a section in the Export Development Act that touches the very root of democracy. Instead of making the authorized capital $2 billion, as in the Bill, this amendment reduces it to $1 billion and $100. While the amendment does not cure the Bill of a very bad precedent, it does make it better than it otherwise would have been.
I want to commend the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) for bringing in this amendment because it touches the very heart of Parliament, which is accountability, responsibility and control of the public purse.
When Parliament was first brought about, everyone appeared to speak there. That was probably the truest Parliament possible since there was direct representation from the people. As societies and populations grew, a method of sending the representative of a number of people was devised, but the basic principle of representing the thinking of the people to the greatest possible degree still remained. We now have one Member representing 50,000, 100,000 and in some places

September 15, 1983
Export Development Act
300,000	people. There is a responsibility for that Member to secure the thinking of the people he represents.
This is done in a number of ways. It is sometimes done through the election process when a Member stands for certain principles and the people support him. But that is not the whole story. 1 believe it is necessary to go to the people periodically to secure their thinking in order that their wishes might be expounded on the floor of the House.
This particular section of the Bill does just the opposite. It gives a group of appointed people the authority to spend money that has not been authorized by the representatives of the people. I say that is basically wrong. We are becoming too far removed from the entire concept of actual parliamentary representation. Many Members now say that they will give leadership and tell the people what is good for them, but that is not democracy. That is what we see in Moscow where the people are told what is good for them whether they like it or not.
Our country has a parliamentary system under which the Government should be reflecting the thinking of the people. 1 want to tell the Hon. Members of the Government that this section does not reflect the thinking of Canadians. The polls have shown that Canadians are heartsore over what has been happening. The present Government is no longer representing what the people want. It has been telling the people what is good for them for a number of years and this Bill is a typical example of where the Government has given authority to a group of appointed people to spend money that has not been authorized by the House of Commons or the Senate. That is basically wrong. That is why I say the Hon. Member for Mississauga South should be commended not only for doing a service to the people who sent him here but to the people of Canada who, in a true democracy, have control of the purse.
It may be asked how this unauthorized borrowing takes place under this section. According to the Bill, the authorized capital is $2 billion. Another section which we are also discussing authorizes the Export Development Corporation to borrow ten times that amount, or $20 billion. That is $20 billion in expenditures which are not authorized by the representatives in Parliament. I feel very strongly about this issue because it is at the very heart of Parliament.
A few months ago I was at the Commonwealth Conference along with the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans). It was an excellent conference. One Sunday the organizers of that conference decided to take us to Runnymede where King John signed the Magna Carta. I was thrilled to have the opportunity to stand on the very ground where King John signed that Magna Carta, the basis of British liberty, and I took pictures of the statue and the actual Magna Carta.
The Magna Carta signing was not in a building as many people believed but out in the open. King John was too smart to let people enclose him in a building. He stayed out in the open where he would have an opportunity to get away. The Government is also leaving an opening to get away, because while the $2 billion must be authorized by Parliament, what about the $20 billion? The Government is just as devious as
King John was in trying to leave a loophole to get away from parliamentary procedure which has made this country great. This Bill goes to the very heart of Parliament.
At Runnymede the barons confronted King John, saying that they did not want him spending money unless he had the representation from the people whose money he was taking. Today, the Government should not be spending money unless it has authorization from the people to whom the money belongs. They or their children will have to pay the debt for generations. I do not know what we can do for those who have not yet been born, but we who are here have the responsibility to make sure that we make the Government accountable. The purpose of this amendment is to make sure that the Government is accountable and that we have control of the public purse.
We have much to do to regain complete control of the public purse. I ask the Minister to let us take this important step in honour of the people of Canada and the Magna Carta, so that we may carry on the thinking of our forefathers who wanted a parliamentary system in this country where the people's views are represented. They did not want a government which tells the people what is good for them, as King John was doing. They did not want a government which said it would spend money that it was not authorized to spend. No matter for what purpose it is, the principle is wrong. All moneys expended by a government should be authorized by the people because it goes to the very heart of Parliament. It is control of the purse that we want and which the Hon. Member for Mississauga South seeks in proposing this amendment.
I see that it is now one o'clock.
