subsubtopic: CROWSNEST PASS RATE-CHANGE IN POSITION OF PROGRESSIVE CONSERVATIVE PARTY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the new leader of the Progressive Conservative Party, the Member for Central Nova (Mr. Mulroney), has a very peculiar vision of the Crowsnest Pass rate. In fact, his position changes from day to day-not necessarily for the better-and this applies to the positions taken by his colleagues as well. During the last race for the leadership of the Progressive Conservative Party, some candidates expressed opinions they must be hard pressed to maintain today, since the Progressive Conservative Party has now taken the position that the Crow's Nest Pass rate must not be changed. For instance, the Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) said during the leadership campaign: We cannot upgrade railway transportation in western Canada if we leave the Crow rate intact. The users' share in the cost of transportation must be increased. As for the newly-elected leader, he also maintained that the Government was on the right track. He said repeatedly that although the then Minister of Transport should be a little more flexible, he was on the right track with Bill C-155. He said that farmers were prepared to pay for improved transportation and that this legislation was gaining acceptance. I would ask them to read again a release from Canadian Press dated May 31 and to explain to Canadians why, although the arguments remain the same, their position has changed. The new leader has shown he has little to offer Canadians in the way of consistency.

Madam Speaker, I would like to express my deep concern for the small business community of this nation which has been hardest hit by the Government's economic mismanagement.
If small business is expected to remain a dynamic and innovative sector of our economy, the serious problems facing small-businessmen must be addressed. They continue to be taxation, government regulations and paperwork, high interest rates, and access to capital.
The record tells all. In the first seven months of 1983, 6,122 businesses were forced into bankruptcy. More jobs have been lost in the small business sector in the last two years than in all other sectors combined. Something must be done to reverse this trend as small business is, and will remain, the lifeline of our economy.

subtopic: U.S.S.R.-CALL FOR RELEASE OF ANATOLY SHCHARANSKY

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Peterson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Economic Development and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Economic Development; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: U.S.S.R.-CALL FOR RELEASE OF ANATOLY SHCHARANSKY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on behalf of the parliamentary group on Soviet Jewry. Conditions for the Jewish community in the Soviet Union deteriorate further. Emigration has slowed to a trickle. Those refused exit visas are harassed, and anti-Semitism is the daily fare of Soviet propaganda.
Our parliamentary group will continue to monitor the plight of Soviet Jews, to work directly with them and, on their behalf, to report on developments and to press the Soviet Government to respect basic principles of human rights.
Today, September 15, marks the halfway point in the prison sentence of Anatoly Shcharansky. He was arrested on March 15, 1978, and falsely and unjustly convicted of alleged spying. He was sentenced to 13 years in prison. Shcharansky's only desire is to be reunited with his wife in his homeland. He is the victim of Soviet efforts to suppress and eradicate all vestiges of Jewish communal life.
Recent events have again heightened distrust of the U.S.S.R. We call on the Soviets to show that they can live by the standards of the international community. We call on the Soviets to free Shcharansky. We pledge our efforts so that Shcharansky and all others like him may enjoy fundamental human rights.

subtopic: U.S.S.R.-CALL FOR RELEASE OF ANATOLY SHCHARANSKY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, before 1 read my statement, may I congratulate the Hon. Member for Willowdale (Mr. Peterson). I am sure all Members of the House welcome his appointment as chairman of the parliamentary group.

The resignation yesterday of Prime Minister Begin of Israel marks the passing of an era. Mr. Begin has lead his Government through a turbulent period in the history of the young State of Israel. Many of us in Canada, like many Israelis, have not always agreed with all of his policies, but we have also noted his many accomplishments. In domestic affairs, for example, he has been instrumental in creating the circumstances in which the Sephardic population of Israel has been able to find its political voice.
Without question, however, Mr. Begin's major accomplishment was to achieve peace with Israel's largest and most important Arab neighbour, Egypt. At Camp David, he, together with the late President Sadat and United States President Carter, persevered in difficulty, lengthy negotiations because they knew that the future of their people and their countries lay in peace, and they were prepared to take the risks and pay the price which peace entailed. Their commitment to

September 15, 1983
peace in the face of obstructions and condemnations led to the signing of a peace treaty after decades of conflict. This historic breakthrough, Madam Speaker, was a gift from Mr. Begin and Mr. Sadat not merely to their own citizens but to the cause of world stability.
Let us salute Mr. Begin, wish him well, and express our hope that his successors will have the strength and the necessary response from their neighbouring countries to carry forward the peace process which Mr. Begin, on Israel's part, began.

subtopic: SIDE EFFECTS OF BIRTH CONTROL PILLS
SIDE EFFECTS OF BIRTH CONTROL PILLS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in April, 1983, a 20-year-old Toronto woman died of complications from the birth control pills she was taking. The complications which led to her death were neither new or unusual. Past experience with the pills indicated that side effects like those which killed this woman were likely to occur in a certain number of users. No one, it seems, told Carol Rosenberg, or perhaps she would be alive today.
It is not enough to expect that doctors and pharmacists will provide patients with adequate information about the possible side effects of the drugs they are given. This would be ideal, but experience has shown that it simply does not work. A recent study found that nearly half of all patients misunderstood the verbal instructions they received about their medications.
The Canadian Pharmaceutical Association produces detailed information sheets about the effects and possible side effects of virtually every drug sold in Canada, but distribution of these sheets by pharmacists is voluntary and more the exception than the rule. The Consumers' Association of Canada has been asking for four years that pharmacists be required to provide this information with each and every prescription they fill. I think it is about time the Government acted on this recommendation.

Madam Speaker, my constituents in Mission-Port Moody regard the unemployment problem as the number one issue in Canada today, and so they should. Some 14,000 people received unemployment insurance benefits in my riding during August. Hundreds more have exhausted their benefits, and many have given up looking for work.
This situation is tearing at the very fabric of our society. Families are suffering, young people are becoming restless, and human discontent is growing. The Government simply continues to dream up band-aid programs. These billion dollar band-aids only mask the real severity of the problem. People do not want short-term jobs just so they can requalify for unemployment insurance. They want long-term work and real pay cheques.
The Canada Works Program announced recently will provide about 15 to 20 jobs in Mission-Port Moody. This is little
September 15, 1983

comfort for the 14,000 unemployed people in my riding. The Canadian people want this Government to call an election so that they can elect a new Government that will stimulate confidence and allow the private sector to create long-lasting jobs.
Hear, hear!

subtopic: UREA FORMALDEHYDE-COST OF REMOVAL FROM HOMES
UREA FORMALDEHYDE-COST OF REMOVAL FROM HOMES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I wish to raise in this House once again the matter of urea formaldehyde foam and call the attention of the House to the fact that the National Home Owners Advisory Council is meeting today in Ottawa.
In spite of the assurances and glib statements of the previous Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs concerning amenities and improvements for people who have urea formaldehyde foam in their homes, the Government has failed in a number of areas to provide a remedy for those suffering from this problem.
The Government promised to pay home owners who had UFF1 removed from their homes an additional $500 grant under the Canadian Home Insulation Program, by the end of 1983. To date, although applications are moving forward, no money has been put up by the Government to cover these applications. It is time that happened.
The second serious omission is that the Government committed itself to providing removal procedures for brick homes, in many of which it cost an exhorbitant amount to remove the material. It has failed to provide any remedy in that area. The last item is that in many homes it is costing far more than the money available, the measly $500 grant, to remove that material. In many homes it is a matter of a health problem, and it is time the Government provided an opportunity under the Income Tax Act to deduct the balance for income tax purposes. It is time the Government fulfilled the commitment it made earlier this year to people with urea formaldehyde foam in their homes, and acted on this very important issue.

subtopic: CALL FOR WITHDRAWAL OF TOBACCO TAX
CALL FOR WITHDRAWAL OF TOBACCO TAX
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, effective September 1, 1983, the federal Government increased taxation on cigarettes by 15.8 per cent. In 1982 more than 60 per cent of the price of a package of cigarettes was made up of federal and provincial taxes. In 1982, here in Ontario, for example, federal and provincial taxes on the manufacturers' wholesale trade price of 36.8 cents were 365 per cent. In 1982 the federal Government received $1.15 billion in cigarette tax. Why a further 15.8 per cent now?
I can tell you why not. First, the tobacco growers receive only six cents of the price for a package of 20. Tax increases will seriously damage the industry and force bankruptcies in this area of agriculture. Second, this increase, along with last year's increase, will cost Canadians upwards of 2,500 jobs at harvest time because of a reduction in sales. Third, personal wages in Canada are now increasing slower than inflation. Fourth, six and five. Where does this 15.8 per cent increase relate to six and five? Lalonde's elastic rule.
1 call on the Government to reconsider this latest tax, look at the detrimental effect on the tobacco industry and employment, and then withdraw it.

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration. It concerns his Department's training and retraining programs which are designed, I would say, more to perpetuate unemployment than to provide jobs. For instance, there is a new program called PATH, for women,

September 15, 1983
Oral Questions
which is to lead to careers in non-traditional areas. In the Kingston area, where there are at the moment 3,000 unemployed women, the PATH Program has just been reduced from 20 to 15 places because only women with a grade 12 or better education can qualify. Similarly, in word processing courses, a woman has to have a 50-word per minute typing speed before she can qualify. Neither of these qualifications is necessary.
When will the Government remove these completely unnecessarily restrictive requirements so that the benefits of retraining and training in these new technologies will not be limited to a chosen few, but made available to the majority of people who will otherwise be condemned to long-term unemployment?

speakeroldname: Hon. John Roberts (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member is incorrect in her general assertion at the beginning of her question. The purpose of these training programs is indeed to train people in skills which will provide them with useful and continuing employment. I am happy to have her representations about specific criteria which she feels are being applied in the Kingston area in a way which is retrogressive. I will be happy to look into those allegations, check to see if there have been changes in the criteria which have been applied, and see whether they are constructively directed. I thank her for her representation.

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, what is happening in Kingston as a community is happening in every community right across the country. The Government's attitude seems to be that if it can just throw a lump of money at retraining, suddenly all of the problems of the unemployed are going to be resolved. Last year, for example, the Government committed approximately $50 million to industrial retraining in Ontario, and $27 million was returned unused. At a time when unemployment is running at half a million in Ontario, only 20,000 people were able to take advantage of that program. Does that not prove to the Minister that the program simply is not working? Why was that $27 million returned unused? Why was it not applied to more people? Has the Minister looked into it? What are the reasons for not taking up that money?

speakeroldname: Hon. John Roberts (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 am a bit puzzled by the Hon. Member's attitude. With one breath she suggests we are not doing enough, and then with another breath she says that our approach seems to be to place money in response to the problem. Of course we are directing funds to the problem because it is an extraordinarily important problem for Canadians.
The Hon. Member asked specifically about the fact that certain funds have not been taken up. The reason, and this has been a factor particularly in Ontario, is because many of the job-training programs require the participation and co-operation of private sector employers to give the training that is required. Having just come out of the recession, many employers find themselves in a constrained financial position and are not able to devote the overhead resources to that kind of training, in their view. Therefore, the reason for the lack of pickup is the reluctance on the part of some people in the private sector to take advantage of the programs at the present time. I very much hope that some of the recent publicity which has been focused on that problem will lead other employers to come forward with proposals and take up the programs that provide the kind of training that is needed.

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, what the Minister does not seem to realize is that the approach of the Government is not working in the field of retraining, no matter what he does. What is needed is a total re-examination of the whole issue.
Other countries are doing much better than Canada in this regard. They seem to be much more imaginative in coming to grips with retraining to meet the challenges of the technological age. I would like to ask the Minister, since I understand that the Cabinet committee on social policy is looking at the British scheme for training and retraining youth, whether or not that program will be introduced here in Canada, and when. Second, has the Minister also looked at the joint industry-government model in Japan to see whether or not their system of industrial workers being allocated 50 days each year for training and retraining could possibly be utilized in Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. John Roberts (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I do not think it is the case that whatever we do will not work. I do think it is true that the Hon. Member will say that whatever we do is not working. The fact is that we are looking at the British example, as she has suggested. 1 would also point out to her that under the Career Access Program there already are job-subsidy programs which assist young people by providing work and training at the same time. That program is already in place under the Access Program and can be utilized for that purpose.
We are, as well, looking at the experience of other countries such as Japan, as she has suggested. 1 am not entirely sure that the Japanese experience can be transported to the Canadian environment. We are looking for ideas and possible programs in every environment, not only the United Kingdom and Japan.
September 15, 1983

subsubtopic: RECOMMENDATION THAT LIBRARIES SHOULD COMPENSATE AUTHORS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Communications who knows, I am sure, that there were demonstrations organized by Canadian authors in a number of cities today. 1 am sure the Minister knows that the average income earned by professional writers in Canada is only $3,000 a year and that many of them are living in poverty. A number of countries in Europe have implemented systems that provide for compensation to authors when public users borrow books from public libraries. This idea has been endorsed by the Applebaum-Heb-ert Commission and by the Canada Council, and in a speech to the authors made by the Minister, some 16 months ago, he indicated support for that idea as well. I wonder if the Minister could tell us when he will do more than talk about it and will begin to implement that policy.

subsubtopic: RECOMMENDATION THAT LIBRARIES SHOULD COMPENSATE AUTHORS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as the Hon. Member has indicated, this is a question that is of interest to me personally. I have indicated my interest, not only to the Writers' Union some months ago, but also to the Federal Cultural Policy Review Committee and to the Provinces.
The Federal Cultural Policy Review Committee has come up with a solution that differs markedly from the proposal made by the Canada Council. As far as the Provinces are concerned, since the Provinces do have jurisdiction over libraries, provincial officials feel that it is a question of importance to them and they have indicated that any scheme that is implemented should only be implemented with the full consent and co-operation of the provincial Governments.
In the meantime the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture has before it the Applebaum-Hebert review committee report with the solution that was propsoed by Applebaum and Hebert. 1 have sought that committee's advice on how we should go about implementing its report. The committee have indeed favoured me with their recommendations regarding broadcasting, and I am very much looking forward to their favouring me with their recommendations regarding the specific plan of fair payment to authors.
I should point out to the hon. gentleman that this is part of the more general problem of ensuring that creators of all kinds, be they authors, sculptors, painters, or producers of

September 15, 1983
Oral Questions
cultural products, be treated fairly in the marketplace and receive a fair return for their creative activities.

subsubtopic: RECOMMENDATION THAT LIBRARIES SHOULD COMPENSATE AUTHORS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, it is unfortunate that when representatives of the Writers' Union met with one of the Minister's very senior officials a few days ago, they got the impression that they were being stonewalled and that very little if anything had been done by the Minister or his Department to put some program in place. The Minister has said that libraries fall under the jurisdiction of the Provinces, but I cannot imagine that any provincial Government would object if the federal Government would fund a program to provide money for authors each time a consumer borrows a book.
Madam Speaker, I would again ask the Minister when the Writers' Union may expect something definite, rather than the kind of runaround and talk which they have been getting from the Minister.

Madam Speaker, I think it is very easy for the hon. gentleman to suggest that the federal Government should simply rush in and put up some additional funds. There are a number of problems involved with that.
As far as the Canada Council is concerned, it has full liberty of action in dispensing its funds in the way that it sees fit. If the Canada Council feels that this is the priority, it can indeed on its own motion set up a fund to pay to the writers. On the other hand, if I were to give funds to the Canada Council and earmark them for this plan, there would be an immediate reaction on the part of the cultural community, and quite properly, to the effect that I was giving policy directions to the Canada Council, something which I obviously ought not be doing.
I am suggesting to the Hon. Member that a number of groups have come up with different solutions to this problem. The Writers' Union has come up with one solution, the Canada Council has come up with a different set of proposals, and the Applebaum-Hebert Report, which is presently in front of the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture, has come up with a different solution.
I would suggest to the Hon. Member that the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture get on with the work of examining that chapter of the Applebaum-Hebert Committee Report, that they examine and analyse the different proposals that have been put before the committee and, having done so, that they make recommendations that the Government will indeed consider.

Madam Speaker, my question is also directed to the Minister of Communications and concerns the same subject. The Minister has indicated that, in his view, there are a number of schemes which need to
be clarified, understood, and decided upon. Surely the Minister is aware, is he not, that the Canada Council, virtually all of the arts and cultural communities in the country, the library associations and everyone who is associated with this proposal, agree that the Minister should implement the proposal put forward by the Union? Is that not true? After ten years of discussion and two years of personal commitment, why is the Minister still stonewalling these people who make, on the average, $ 1,000 per year?

Madam Speaker, indeed, I am very interested in learning the position of the Hon. Member. As I told him before, I brought this whole matter up at the federal-provincial conference. There is an obvious interest on the part of the Provinces. If I could implement a scheme which would affect the National Library of Canada, I do not think it would be a solution to the problem. The main users and those responsible for libraries are the Provinces.
If a scheme is to be introduced, it should obviously take the provincial interest into account. Obviously the Provinces, which put money into the libraries, ought to make a contribution to setting up the scheme. That is why I brought the matter to the attention of my provincial colleagues in May, 1982, when 1 asked for their opinion on how such a scheme should be implemented. I am willing to pursue the matter with them.
I would also suggest that it is not good enough to say that a scheme ought to be implemented; I say to the Hon. Member that he and his colleagues who were Members of the Standing Committee on Culture and Communications should look at the scheme proposed by the Writers' Union of Canada, the proposal of the Canada Council, and the proposal of the Applebaum-Hebert Commission. If I were to go ahead and implement a proposal that differed from them in some way, I am sure the Hon. Member would be the first to say that I had not consulted Parliament before devising a scheme, that 1 had complete disregard for the Applebaum-Hebert Commission report. That report is presently before the committee of which the Hon. Member, as critic for his Party, is a member.

Madam Speaker, the Minister hid behind the Applebaum-Hebert Commission report for two years without implementing the proposal. If he refers to page 207 of that report he will see that the Commission is on record as urging him to implement any proposal rather than no proposal.
It is not my position that these people are interested in; it is the Minister's position. That is why they allege the Minister reneged on his commitment. The Applebaum-Hebert Commission wants the Minister to do this; why doesn't he?

Madam Speaker, it is basically because a number of options are open to us. The copyright legislation is an option. It is one that
September 15, 1983_______________________ COMMONS
many people wish to cast aside, however, because if this right were put in the copyright legislation, payment would be made to all authors, independent of nationality. Our interest is in devising a scheme which will bring greater returns to Canadian writers. That is the objective of the exercise.
The Hon. Member suggests that I implement any proposal-that any proposal is better than no proposal. 1 suggest to the Hon. Member that a reasonable proposal would obviously require provincial participation. A proposal that does not include provincial participation is not, to my mind, a reasonable proposal.

The House resumed consideration of Bill C-110, to amend the Export Development Act, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs; and Motions Nos. 3 and 5 (Mr. Blenkarn).

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I believe the Hon. Member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Kilgour) has the floor.

Mr. Speaker, to refresh Members's memories, let me read Motion No. 3:
That Bill C-l 10, an Act to amend the Export Development Act, be amended in Clause 5 by striking out lines 23 to 26 at page 3 and substituting the following therefor:
11.(1) The authorized capital of the Corporation is one billion one hundred dollars divided into ten million and one shares with a par value of one hundred dollars each.
Motion No. 5 reads:
That Bill C-l 10, an Act to amend the Export Development Act, be amended in Clause 7 by striking out lines 39 to 41 at page 3 and lines 1 and 2 at page 4 and substituting the following therefor:
14. The aggregate amount of borrowings of the Corporation pursuant to sections 12 and 13 shall not exceed the amount equal to ten times the aggregate of the paid in capital and earned surplus in the accounts of the Corporation.
The explanation of this, as I see it, may be stated quite simply. The Government proposes, as you will know, Sir, that there be $2 billion in authorized capital for the corporation and that the aggregate amount of borrowing of the corporation shall "not exceed an amount equal to ten times the authorized capital of the corporation". Therefore, if you put the Government's proposal against our amendments, the Government proposes to allow the corporation to borrow $20 billion without further parliamentary authorization. That is the basis of our strong objection, the objection taken by other Members in the debate-
[ Translation]
-and that is the essence of my speech. The position taken by our caucus, Mr. Speaker, is that the authority to allow expen-
September 15, 1983

ditures as vast as those we are discussing today should remain with Parliament. It is up to us, as elected representatives of the Canadian people, to vote on the monies that are to be spent as proposed in this Bill.

The fundamental objection which the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) has made is that there is no parliamentary control on contributions. The Government just puts in money, any amount of money up to $2 billion, and then it has the absolute right to subscribe to the capital of the EDC and there will be no further voting upon it. Whether or not the EDC receives the money from the Government without our amendment-that is up to the $2 billion-this measure would give the EDC the right to borrow on the credit of our country to the extent of $20 billion. We say-

-this kind of accounting, if you will, cannot be tolerated if our country's finances are to be at all sound.

We say that if we pass this Bill the EDC-1 do not think there is a Member in this House who has anything but support for the EDC in its concept of assisting the exporting of goods-can borrow $20 billion to finance any sort of project. In passing, let me mention the Algerian project which was the subject at a television program shown last week, CTV'S W5. The project, as I understand it, is basically a monument to the Algerian revolution financed by the Canadian taxpayers through the EDC by an enormous subsidy in terms of interest rates. I wish every Canadian could have seen W5 and heard the comments made by the EDC spokesman. It is an example for each and every one of us that instead of giving $2 billion carte blanche we should be showing greater parliamentary control over what the EDC will be doing in the years ahead.
Let me also cite in support of this amendment a study done by the Economic Council of Canada in 1982 entitled "A Study of Government Credit and Credit Guarantees to the Private Sector". On page 60 the conclusion in the relevant section reads:
We have noted that there are in general few deficiencies in the markets for these instruments.
Speaking about credit insurance and the like:
The private sector, however, could be encouraged to fill the remaining gaps through a reorientation of EDC activities towards reinsurance and refinancing. Disregarding the support accorded by foreign countries to their own exports, more appropriate instruments than subsidized export credit could be used to achieve the government's macroeconomic objectives. Although it would be desirable for all countries to abandon simultaneously their export subsidy program, this seems improbable at the moment and Canada must continue to offer export subsidies for strategic reasons.

-by Professor Andre Raynauld who I see is the president-elect of that professional body of economists, the Economic Association of Canada. He is a former Chairman of the Economic Council of Canada and a former Liberal MNA in the Quebec National Assembly. Speaking about the EDC, Professor Raynauld said, "It is rapidly becoming a bureaucratic monster, borrowing and lending money, making unsound loans to foreign countries, extending its empire and involving Canada in transactions and negotiations that are both costly and inefficient." I understand from my colleague for Mississauga South that Professor Raynauld goes on in his study to compare our Export Development Corporation with like corporations and agencies in other exporting countries and does not draw favourable conclusions.
Many points have been made in this debate and I am trying not to duplicate them, but let me touch on the question of authorized capital. Normally a trust or a loan company is entitled to lend a multiple of its subscribed capital and earned surplus. EDC does not have that type of limitation. Its limitation is a multiple of authorized capital. As I mentioned before, the consequence of this, if our amendment does not pass, and even if it does to a limited extent, is that it does not matter at all how much money the Government in fact contributes as capital to the corporation; borrowings are a multiple of the capital authorization. The effect of the Government's proposal here would be to increase the authorized capital to $2 billion, so that its authorized borrowing can then be $20 billion. Our amendment is simply to reduce the capital to $1 billion from $2 billion and to try to limit the amount of unauthorized-that is, unauthorized by Parliament-borrowing that the EDC may do.
1 urge Members opposite to support us so that Parliament can, in a small way, reassert its control over the public purse.

Mr. Speaker, in joining in the debate on the amendment now under consideration, I want to emphasize for all Members who have not had an opportunity to date to read the provisions of Bill C-110 how vitally important the amendment we are now discussing is to the whole operation of the Export Development corporation. I say that because it has become almost usual in dealing with the Government with which we now live with Canada to talk in terms of a billion dollars or half a billion dollars. It is not as it was, perhaps ten years ago, a matter of sinking in to the Members of this House the money grab that the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan) is attempting to make in the Bill before us.
The money grab I am referring to is, of course, what my colleague commented on, the provision we are now dealing with calling for a total capitalization in the Export Development Corporation of $2 billion. When you multiply that by ten, and that is the way this Bill works, you are considering that the Government is asking for $20 billion of lending authority, which in turn means borrowing authority. Let us never forget that. A government cannot lend a nickel without

September 15, 1983
Export Development Act
raising it from the taxpayers of this country or borrowing. We are considering $20 billion of borrowing authority to be lent to various concerns around the world. That is what is before us.
Members should take the time to read this Bill. I notice that the socialists are not even getting into this debate. That is typical of them. They have no appreciation of money when it is not their own. As long as it is taxpayers' money or debt rolling, they somehow remain mute in this House. They could not care less. It is time that we fingered that irresponsible group which they are in this House and throughout the nation.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. While the Member berates us, I wonder if he would stand and honestly acknowledge the fact-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. 1 do not think it would be helpful for me to remind the Hon. Member what might constitute a point of order. However, I must indicate to him that debate is not a point of order, and that is what he is entering into.

You are a good Speaker, Mr. Speaker.
I am trying to press Hon. Members to take an active interest in the amendment under consideration. To put it into perspective let me say that when we are talking about a $2 billion capitalization for the Export Development Corporation, it in turn triggers $20 billion of available funds. The Government of Canada would either have to borrow those funds or otherwise raise the money. That $20 billion is to be re-lent to other people.
Let us put this into perspective. Perhaps the most relevant country to look at is the United States of America. It has an institution that might be compared to the Export Development Corporation called the Export-Import Bank of the United States. Looking at the September, 1981 statement, we see that the total paid-in capital of the United States counterpart to the Export Development Corporation is $1 billion. This Government is asking the people of Canada, through this Parliament, to accept as an authorized capital for our corporation, for openers, twice the size of the total paid-in capital of the comparable institution in the United States, the Export-Import Bank in 1981.
The United States is 10 or 11 times the size of Canada in terms of Gross National Product. One would think that an institution there, with money resources such as this Government wants for the Export Development Corporation, would have capital of $10 billion. In fact, it has $1 billion in capitalization.
My second point is that not only is the capital in the Export-Import Bank in the United States in the fiscal year September, 1981, only half of what this Government feels it needs in its gluttony and greed, but the total of its borrowed funds is $16 billion. In the clauses now under review, we are considering an authorization of capital of $2 billion, a total commitment of $20 billion, which is twice the total paid-in capital of the Export-Import Bank in the United States in 1981. In gross terms, the $20 billion figure is approximately 25
per cent larger than the total outstanding commitment of the Export-Import Bank in the United States in 1981.
I hope I have put this into perspective. Surely all of us in this House agree in principle that if we can have a plan to increase exports from Canada to the countries of the world, we should support it. Nobody is challenging that. The real question is twofold. First, can we do it and ensure that Parliament can keep control of the spending that is entailed in the program? Second, can we do it in the most efficient way possible? Let me touch on those two questions.
If the amendment that my colleague is suggesting is not accepted, reducing the authorized capital from $2 billion to $1 billion, which is still 50 per cent more than paid-in capital in the American counterpart, it will mean that that extra half billion dollars multiplied by ten, which is $5 billion, is to all intents and purposes lost from the control of this House. In the name of Canadian taxpayers, what is wrong with us as Members of Parliament saying, "It may be that in future you will need an extra $5 billion, but do not ask us to give you the blank cheque on September 15, 1983. We will give you the running money you may feel is needed for the coming months or years, but come back to the ultimate authority, the House of Commons and the Parliament of Canada and ask once again for that extra $5 billion. Don't expect us to simply give it to you without questions asked." That is what this debate is all about.
1 would suggest that if the Export Development Corporation's American counterpart, the Export-Import Bank of the United States, can get by and can break into the world export markets to the extent that it has without the type of capital that is being contemplated in the Bill that is now before us, surely it behooves us to turn to the Government and simply ask, why it cannot do likewise. Why does it need such lavish financing from the Parliament of Canada when its main competitor in the United States has much less?
The Minister of State for International Trade is shaking his head. I would like to ask him if he has taken it upon himself to go to the Export-Import Bank of the United States. Has he personally talked to its executives to find out how they can operate in such an effective way by getting levered exports as compared to the over-financing that our Export Development Corporation often engages in? It is my understanding, Mr. Speaker, that the present Minister of State for International Trade has not done so. I understand that, in learning his job, he has not seen fit to make the most obvious comparison with the counterpart to the Export Development Corporation in the United States.
If I had more time, Mr. Speaker, I would like to let Members know where the money that will possibly be authorized with the passage of this Bill will actually go. Who gets the benefit of it? Who are the chosen indirect recipients of these funds? Many of us would be most startled to hear who is on that list, but I see that my time has run out. I would only ask that, before we in the Opposition meekly pass the provision
September 15, 1983

that we are asked to pass and before Government Members who are like trained seals pass it, we bear in mind that it is just not needed. It is like signing a blank cheque on behalf of every taxpayer in the country. We have seen from past experience how irresponsible the Government has been when handling people's funds. Let us not give it more than it absolutely needs.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to place a few comments on the record respecting this Bill and specifically the amendment that is before the House this afternoon. The question of the need for more exports is not at issue. Anyone who has seen the effect that exports have had on the Canadian market will see that the evidence is fairly clear that we are without question a major trading nation and that that has a very direct effect on the wellbeing of every Canadian. That matter is not at issue.
I would also suggest, Mr. Speaker, that it is not at issue that Canadians endorse every effort made by Government to increase, enhance and encourage exports from Canadian manufacturers and primary resources. Those of us who are from agricultural regions, specifically those from western Canada, are constantly made aware of the effect of Government participation on the sale of primary products, be they forest products or agricultural projects. So the second issue that is not in question is the matter of the need, and in fact the desirability, for Government to encourage that economic activity.
It is clear, though, Mr. Speaker, that the export world has become more sophisticated. I would suggest that the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan) take a look at our embassies and consulates abroad. I am sure he is aware of the fact that it is no longer sufficient that we simply have as part of that operation a trading arm only, but rather that it must become much more specific in terms of the commodities or the products involved.
Additionally, the world of trade is, without question, being affected by the world economy today. In fact, many of the world's economies are having difficulty or have gone through a period of difficulty now that recovery has started to take hold. Various protectionist attitudes and measures and non-tariff barriers have become part and parcel of the export business in the last year. Those have always been present, but 1 think, particularly since the last GATT negotiation, that we have seen a much greater proliferation of non-tariff barriers, for example, than those agreed to through the GATT. One needs only point out as an example the difficulties that occurred with the negotiations relative to agricultural products which go back to the early days of GATT and which have always been a strong area of contention. The argument has always been made that each area of the world would like to have the right to self-sufficiency in food production.
There are certain factors with which all of us would agree. However, the question that is before the House today in this amendment is whether or not the amount of money requested, $20 billion, which would increase the borrowing capacity of the Export Development Corporation, is being requested and scrutinized in the proper manner. For example, I do not know
Export Development Act
how amenable the Minister is to changes that would provide that funds requested would come under closer scrutiny of Parliament. I believe that the Minister, with his experience as former Premier of a Province in Canada and now as a Minister of the Crown, is aware that Canadians have raised very serious, substantial and, I believe, valid concerns regarding the accountability not only of Government and its departments and its operations but specifically of what has literally become a spin-off of Government, namely, Crown corporations and, in this case, the Export Development Corporation.
Canadians are asking a very serious question, and that is, how best to control not only the increased numbers of corporations but in fact the money that these corporations are able to borrow in the name of Canadian citizens. It is very difficult for Canadians to understand their total indebtedness as Canadians when one factors in the indebtedness or liabilities that Canadians have toward Crown corporations. For example, the Minister knows that every time his Estimates come before the House, he must appear before a parliamentary committee. He is grilled at that committee, although some of us would suggest insufficiently, but the process does take place and at least there is some accountability to Parliament of the moneys to be expended.
Some of us who have looked at parliamentary procedures argue that a procedure should be put into place that would look at possible expenditures before the fact. The Huntington-Lachance exercise in parliamentary reform is one such attempt to create a model that would allow us to judge before moneys are spent whether or not moneys spent on certain projects could not in fact be spent more wisely.
What is before us today is another attempt by the Government to carry liabilities which are totally on the backs of the Canadian public without addressing the concern had by the Canadian public for accountability. I feel, and I am sure every Member in the House and most Canadians would agree, that the attempts made by Ministers to reach accountability within their own departments is an ongoing and difficult task as Government has grown, but it is of even greater difficulty for Members of the Opposition, and specifically the Canadian public, to find out what the total liability of Canadians is, not only from Government but from Crown corporations as well.
I would urge the Minister to examine the points that have been made and address himself to those points and seriously to consider how amendments could be brought forward that would give some accountability back to the Canadian public, specifically in the Bill before us.
That is not the only area of accountability that should be examined through seed money for corporations or small businesses too start up. Governments have a role-unfortunately, I think to great a role-in choosing winners and losers in the corporate field. Too often it is small corporations unknown to the Government and run by individuals of tremendous entrepreneurial spirit that do not get any Government help. This may be because they have not asked for any, or have not asked

September 15, 1983
Export Development Act
in the correct way or they are not known to Government. Other corporations that appear here constantly asking for grants, loan guarantees and so forth, may not do much to create jobs.
The glaring example of this for almost all Canadians, Mr. Speaker, is the Maislin bail out. That did not create jobs for Canadians. The $34 million that was put into the corporation might have done a great deal for a small corporation or for the Canadian trucking industry. Why should we protect jobs in the United States through that company?
I am concerned about how we can address the question of accountability in the Bill. 1 am tired of Ministers coming before the House at Question Period and in committee saying, "That is a question we cannot answer because a Crown corporation is concerned. When it comes before the committee, then ask the question." Ministers should be responsible; they should have accountability.
The amendment that has been proposed addresses that question, Mr. Speaker. If that amendment is not acceptable to the Minister, I suggest to him that any amendment is acceptable to us which brings back accountability to the Minister and to the House.

Mr. Speaker, 1 agree with the Progressive Conservative motion. This motion is very important to democracy and to the Parliament of Canada. [English]
As the Hon. Member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) says, the important thing about the amendment before the House is the matter of accountability. I think it is time for a lot more accountability from Crown corporations in this country. It is time for more accountability when it comes to giving power to Members of Parliament to scrutinize Crown corporations.
The Province that the Hon. Member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake (Mr. Anguish) and I come from, has a special committee of the legislature which is called a Crown Corporations Committee. The annual reports of Crown corporations are referred to that Committee and the heads of those corporations are called in and questioned. In that way the activities of the corporations are scrutinized and votes are held on whether they are doing the right and proper thing. That is the kind of practice that should be followed at the national level.
The amendment before the House is a small step in that direction. It limits the borrowing that the Export Development Corporation can make without coming back to Parliament. As drafted by the Government, the Bill would allow the Government to borrow up to $20 billion before coming back to the House for approval. The effect of the amendment would be to reduce the authorized capital from $2 billion to $1 billion, and that is a step in the right direction.
In this country, Crown corporations have played a very important role and will continue to do so. We have a lot of them and we need them. The important thing about them is that they must be accountable and more responsive to the
wishes and needs of the country. Crown corporations like the CNR and others are very distant from the Parliament of Canada.
I suggest that, as has been the case in Saskatchewan, we refer the annual reports of Crown corporations to the relevant committee. The CNR annual report goes to the Transport Committee, and so does the Air Canada annual report. Perhaps we should do the same thing with all the other Crown corporations so that we could scrutinize them carefully.
The other thing that I believe we need is a reformation of this institution so that Members and committees have more power to direct Crown corporations to do what they think is best. We should have some power over setting their priorities and agendas and we should be able to work with them on important issues of the day. I think that is an important step that must be taken.

Our country needs a more democratic system. Mr. Speaker, I think that the Right Hon. Prime Minister and the Prime Minister's Office have too much power and the same applies to the Privy Council and the Executive. This is certainly too much power for a majority Government, because with a majority Government, it is the Government that does practically everything there is to be done in the country, without any recognition for the importance of the common Member of Parliament-

-before looking at the point of view of an Opposition Party or whatever.
For these reasons I think we should support the motion that is before the House and try to make Crown corporations more accountable to the public. In saying that, 1 take nothing away from the importance of Crown corporations. We need the Export Development Corporation and we should strengthen it. Canada must become more aggressive in promoting exports. In many ways we are the boy scouts of world trade, not nearly as aggressive as the Germans, the Americans, the French and the Japanese. Our share of world trade has fallen drastically in the last 20 years. If I remember correctly, we used to have about 4 per cent of world trade, and now we have about 2 per cent. For these reasons we must become increasingly aggressive.
In the past, the Export Development Corporation has often assisted larger enterprises and forgotten some of the smaller enterprises. I need only remind you, Mr. Speaker, that about 60 per cent of jobs in Canada are provided by small business. That shows how important it is that small enterprises be promoted. If there is a healthy small business climate, then a lot more jobs will be created for Canadians.
All this could be achieved more easily if we had greater accountability for Crown corporations and a better reflection of the country in the board of directors. There must be greater co-operation between the federal Government and the Provinces and a better approach to trade and exports. This amendment would go some way to make the EDC a better Crown corporation.

Mr. Speaker, in the years that I have been in the House of Commons I have watched the emphasis of interest shift. Sometimes it has been on international affairs, sometimes on energy, at other times on the environment. When the tide of public interest on issues shifts, that is where Parliament tends to focus.
1 think that focus is well placed in this particular Bill. For the past two years the focus has been on the economy. It is one thing to talk about the tragedies of the economy as we have done again and again, but 1 think we must start looking for ways to correct our economic ills.
This focus is not only demonstrated in the House of Commons. This summer the Premiers met and a clear message came out of their consultations. That was, that we must concentrate on international trade. If we are going to work our way out of provincial deficits and national deficits, if we are going to maintain the standard of living we have become accustomed to, it is going to be in this field of trade. The message from that sounding board of our Premiers is a correct message. Their focus in the economy on trade and the itinerant reality of exports is important to all of us, to be wary of, to be aware of, and to enact such Bills as this particular Bill.
Like everyone else who has spoken, I speak in favour of the principle of the Bill. I am in favour of the motherhood issue of exports and of increasing those exports by as many means as we can find. Economists throughout the western world, no matter whether it is Canada, the United States, Britain or France, have brought back into our economic vocabulary the words "productivity" and "growth". A decade ago the words "productivity" and "growth" were out. Those were bad words. We were in an energy crisis. We were in an environmental crisis. Therefore, those were "downer" words and did not receive any emphasis. Today, however, they are respectable words.
How are we going to create more jobs in Canada if we do not increase our productivity? How are we going to sustain the jobs we have? Therefore, we must increase our productivity. We must increase the development of new industries and growth in the industries we already have onstream. But what are we going to do with an increased productivity, an increased growth, how are we going to create and sustain these jobs, if, in fact, we cannot sell in international markets the products of our efforts? Therefore, again we come back to this all-important word "exports". 1 am in favour of increasing exports from Canada. I am willing to do almost anything. There is, however, one thing which I will not export, and that is my democracy. 1 will not export my responsibility to the people who sent me here. 1 will not export my accountability in this House of Commons. And that is what this Bill is doing.
I know the Minister is an enthusiastic and energetic Minister of Trade. I have seen that enthusiasm. I know he has been in politics many, many years. I am sure that on some days like today he feels it is too many, it is too long, it goes on and on. He wants to get on with the business and he wants to expand
Export Development Act
his ideas. However, in that impatience which comes in dealing in a democracy and with a democracy, he must not allow this further erosion. I know this Minister knows the delicacy of the democratic structure. I was in India with him when there was an emergency. He saw the emergency. He saw how a government went a little too far in its hurry, perhaps, to go in the right direction. We cannot let the very, very important democratic principles which he has stood for and, I believe, continues to stand for, be brushed aside for the sake of expediency. He cannot allow that to happen to him. An uprooting of the democratic mode of accountability is found in this Bill.
I remember not too many years ago, as a younger politician, hearing someone make the statement, "What is a million dollars?" We have now gone from "What is a million dollars?", to "What is a billion dollars?", and today we are standing in the House and saying, "What is S10 billion? Just give it to them." For what? For export. We are all for exports, but that is not good enough for me. As much as I like this Minister, as much as 1 do not trust this Government, or do trust this Government, 1 certainly cannot write a blank cheque like this for any purpose no matter how good the cause. Even if it is a cause of humanity, a cause of aid, 1 must still know, if I write that cheque, that in fact there is a measure of accountability which 1 can be responsive to and responsible for. That is not going to happen in this particular Bill, as far as I can see.
Before 1 came here 1 started out as a young, idealistic teacher. I used to teach history in school. Maybe it was because of the political instincts 1 had, but when it came to the section on democracy, 1 taught it with a very special verve because I felt so strongly about it. I can remember going back in that old history book and talking about how the king had all the power and how it must be taken from him by the Magna Carta and how we exchanged, for the right of giving him money, the capacity to gain control and accountability. Accountability, how? Through a House of Commons, through a Parliament. We talked about that word "Parliament", a place to speak, a place to be accountable. That particular accountability evolved to our parliamentary structure, our parliamentary system. However, 1 have watched, and I am watching in this Bill, not the evolution of Parliament, not a Parliament where the people of the nation have a chance for accountability and to speak, not an evolution to see that power grow, but in fact that power being taken away from us. It passes from the king to Parliament, and then from Parliament it is passed back to the Cabinet, then from the Cabinet it is passed back to the Prime Minister. That is bad enough, because our whole system has gone that way, back to a prime ministerial type of government, a government of the PMO. But we are moving this one out even beyond the PMO. Mr. Speaker, I think that many of us would be pleased if the Hon. Member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake would begin his leadership campaign immediately. It would advance the cause of his Party tremendously from its present position in the Gallup poll.
1 would like to speak to the Bill because that is why 1 originally sought your attention this afternoon. The motion before the House would reduce the amount of authorized capital of the Export Development Corporation from its requested two billion one hundred dollars to one billion one hundred dollars divided into ten million and one shares with a par value of $100 each. The purpose of this is also, in the process, to restrain the total amount of moneys that can be guaranteed by the Export Development Corporation by way of secured loans to $10 billion, roughly speaking, rather than $20 billion. The whole objective of the amendment as put forward by the Progressive Conservative Opposition is to make the Export Development Corporation more responsible and accountable to Parliament and to restrain it in some of the exercises of exuberance which, in fact, in some cases, have not
produced a net balance of trade in favour of Canada but, rather, have represented a net cost to the taxpayers of Canada.
1 want to use the balance of my time to illustrate my point by referring to one case which 1 will preface by a recent comment made by Professor Andre Raynaud of the University of Montreal, who said that the Export Development Corporation
-is rapidly becoming a bureaucratic monster, borrowing and lending money, making unsound loans to foreign countries, extending its empire and involving Canada in transactions and negotiations that are both costly and inefficient.
Yesterday I made the point that we must decide whether the Export Development Corporation is to be first and foremost interested in advancing Canada's opportunities around the world, which is an important goal in these difficult economic times, or whether it is to be an instrument of foreign aid. The case I want to use to illustrate what 1 consider to be the hastiness and secrecy which we in this House sometimes find so repulsive, is one involving the financing of two major projects in Ireland. One involves the construction of an aluminum refinery by Alcan Ireland, and the second involves the opening of a new copper-zinc mine in the country of Ireland by Tara Mines Limited, which is affiliated with Cominco Inc. These two projects were first initiated in 1975 and 1976. In the case of the Alcan smelter, it is just now coming on to line largely because of a number of serious labour problems and delays which have occurred throughout the construction phase.
Therefore, when these two projects were brought to my attention by a constituent back in 1979, I wrote to the President of the Export Development Corporation, Mr. Syl-vain Cloutier, to provide more details as to who was the recipient of the Canadian work that was being financed with some $30.6 million in the case of the Alcan project and $30 million in the case of the Tara Mines project. I asked if he would provide an inventory of the Canadian recipients, some idea as to regional distribution in Canada and the benefits to be gained by Canada in relation to the cost of guaranteeing or the risks of guaranteeing this amount of money, some $60 million. I did so because my constituent, who had formerly been a citizen of Ireland, had lost, with his father, the family business because of the labour instability which he had experienced in Ireland.
I will not make a value judgment as to whether Ireland is a more or less secure place in which to invest from the point of view of labour stability than Canada, but I might say, as reflected in a letter which I wrote to Mr. Cloutier in 1980, that under the Trade Union act of Ireland (1906), trade unions in Ireland are immune from any court action being lodged against them for a violation of labour contracts. My constituent, who had lost his business because of some rather nasty problems relating to an attempt to unionize the family business, asked the question as to whether Canada had considered the risk to Canadian capital in seeing it used to finance a major aluminum refinery, in that case, which would, at the same time, present additional competition to our major Alcan smelter at Kittimat in British Columbia and the anticipated expansion of Alcan's activities in Manitoba. My constituent
September 15, 1983

was concerned as to whether the Export Development Corporation had considered that this capital might be at considerable risk because, as his experience at least had shown, many businesses and industries in Ireland had been disrupted by illegal labour walkouts against which there was no defence or recourse before the courts of Ireland.
1 do not know if the allegations are true, but I think it is important that we have an opportunity to consider questions of this nature before the House before major amounts of money are put at risk in other nations. More important, I think that we should have an opportunity in each major project of this sort to examine the officials of the Export Development Corporation or the Minister responsible as to the costs and benefits that are entailed in each one of these major undertakings.
Therefore, in my letter to Mr. Cloutier, dated August 21, 1980, I stated: "In view of the ongoing labour strife within the Republic of Ireland", which at that time had already delayed the project by many months, "and in particular the extended labour dispute which has closed the Alcan mining site at Aughnish Island in the County of Limerick, I must put to you the following questions".
These are the questions that I addressed to Mr. Cloutier:
1)	What is the total value of all loans which have been extended by EDC to industrial ventures in the Republic of Ireland?
2)	Will you provide me with an inventory of all goods and services provided by Canadian firms in relation to these guaranteed loans, and will you also provide me with an unequivocal assurance that all such funds guaranteed by Canada have been used to finance purchases from Canada?
3)	Have all repayments been made regularly and in accordance with the original terms of agreement relating to each of these EDC sponsored loans?
I must say that Mr. Cloutier was quite prompt in his reply but he was very superficial in the terms of the nature of the information he gave me. As most Crown corporation presidents do, he gave me the usual gobble-de-gook about what a great institution he was in charge of and about all the great benefits it created for the Canadian people.
However, when it came to answering my questions I received no information other than that Canada had guaranteed loans for a total of $60.6 million and an assurance which I will read from the relevant paragraph. He stated:
I can assure you that EDC closely controls the financing and ensures that payments are made to the Canadian exporter for the goods and services for which financing is made available.
It is rather revealing when Mr. Cloutier continues to state:
In order to respect the commercial confidentiality of the Canadian companies involved, we are unable to provide you with a detailed list of the Canadian suppliers; however, some of the major items supplied to these projects from Canada include grinding mills, compressors, steam generators, filters, instruments, conveyor systems, valves, pumps, electrical equipment, structural steel and engineering and design services.
The President concluded by stating:
I hope this information will be of use to you.
As they usually assure us:
If there is anything further you may wish, I would be glad to hear from you.
